messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran is a 48-year-old married woman who has spent most of her adult life building a quiet, orderly life in the United States. She works as a tutor, usually meeting middle school and high school students in their homes, at a library study room, or online. The violence that brought her to treatment came from a man she had once trusted deeply, a former romantic partner from before her marriage. Near the end of that relationship, an argument in his apartment turned physical. What stays with her is not a smooth story but flashes: his face changing, the glint of a heavy metal object on a nearby table, the bathroom mirror catching a partial reflection of him moving toward her, the feeling that she had nowhere to go. Even now, when she tries to speak about it, the memory comes in disconnected pieces, more like separate photographs than a continuous account, and each image carries the same surge of terror she felt then.

In the months that followed, Linh found herself reaching conclusions about what the assault meant about the world and about herself. She had come to believe that you can never really know who will harm you, because someone who had once seemed loving had become dangerous without warning. She was certain something in her had been permanently altered for the worse; she no longer felt like the composed, trusting woman she had been before. There was also a quieter but painful conviction that she was now fundamentally set apart from other people, an outsider carrying something other people could not see. Those beliefs gave the memories a grim permanence. When fragments of the assault returned, they did not feel like old material surfacing and passing; they seemed to confirm, again and again, that the world was unsafe and that she had been changed beyond repair.

Her body also began responding to danger cues with startling speed. In ordinary settings she became superalert, watchful in a way that exhausted her. Often her body reacted before she had time to think; her chest tightened, her shoulders braced, and she was already scanning the room before she had consciously identified why. In those moments, the old images came back fast. A sharp reflection in a window, the sight of a man shifting his weight near a doorway, or a heavy object left on a desk could pull up one of those frozen visual fragments and with it the same terror, as if her nervous system were retrieving the event ahead of her mind.

Because the memories arrived this way, Linh gradually organized her life around preventing surprise. She began constantly checking her surroundings for signs of threat. Mirrors became especially important to her. If she entered a student’s home for tutoring, she would quickly note where reflective surfaces were and catch herself checking them repeatedly, wanting to know who was behind her and whether anyone was moving toward her without her seeing. She also became acutely vigilant toward people, especially men whose moods felt unreadable to her. The disconnected, photographic flashes of the assault made her feel that danger came suddenly and from just outside the edge of awareness, so she tried to stay one step ahead of it.

Over time, those habits strengthened the sense that threat was everywhere. The more she scanned rooms, tracked exits, and noticed reflective surfaces, the more potential danger she found. In any environment she automatically identified objects that could be used as weapons—a letter opener on a parent’s desk, a metal lamp in a study room, kitchen knives visible from the dining table where she was tutoring. Her watchfulness did not calm her; it kept her on guard. By searching constantly for what could go wrong, she taught herself that there was always something to brace against, and her body remained primed to react before she had fully taken in what was happening.

This has begun to constrict her work and marriage. She still tutors, but she prefers online sessions and feels tense when she has to go into unfamiliar homes. She positions herself so she can see doors and reflections, which some parents have noticed, and she worries she appears odd or rude. At home, she does not speak much about the assault, but her husband has seen her startle and look past him into mirrors or windows, as if checking who else might be there. When memories break through now, they again arrive as vivid, disconnected pictures charged with terror, and each return seems to prove to her that she is damaged and separate from other people in a lasting way.

Linh finally sought help after a tutoring session in which she caught sight of herself in a hallway mirror and, in the same instant, noticed a heavy stapler on a table behind her. Her body jolted before she could think, and for a moment she was back in those photographic fragments. What frightened her most was not only the terror itself but the fear that this is who she is now: someone permanently on guard, permanently changed. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is that the memories might one day feel like something that happened rather than something that is still waiting to happen.
